newsitem.title: UK: UK's Bottomley defends BT entertainment ban.
newsitem.headline: UK's Bottomley defends BT entertainment ban.

text.p: Britain's National Heritage Secretary Virginia Bottomley said on Tuesday the government was right to restrict British Telecommunications Plc in providing entertainment services.
She said the rule would remain in place until 2001 and the goalposts would not be shifted.
"It would be wrong to tear that up," she told the National Heritage Select Committee in parliament. "What confidence would that give other investors?"
The committee feared that BT, deprived of revenue from entertainment television, would not invest sufficiently in the necessary technology and would fall behind the pace.
Labour MP Gerald Kaufman, chairman of the committee, asked if the government's policy was not a case of obsession with inward investment crowding out internal investment -- from BT.
Bottomley said the regulation had already prompted huge investment from the cable industry and billions of pounds of that investment would be put at risk if the current framework was not maintained.
"Industry needs to be confident it will benefit from its investments without the government arbitrarily changing the ground rules," she said.

She also rejected the idea that BT would be left behind. "BT is already investing in the digital world in a number of areas. The idea that their skill and ability is being shut out of this market is ludicrous."

Last week, British pay television operator BSkyB said it would press ahead with plans to launch a 200-channel digital satellite service later this year. And the Cable Communications Association says digital cable television will offer up to 1,000 channels.
